procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Assam & Nagaland High Court in Cr. Revision No. 31 of 1967 dated May 23, 1969, which revised the charges framed by the Special Judge and quashed them.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent filed a revision petition in the High Court of Assam and Nagaland against the framing of charges against him by the Special Judge. The High Court allowed the revision and quashed the charges.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Delhi Special Police Establishment, New Delhi, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution against the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'liable to be tried' in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code refers to the initial jurisdiction of a court to take cognizance of a case, or its jurisdiction to decide the case on its merits.

law.fact_text: Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) is designed to avoid conflicts of jurisdiction for offences that are triable by both ordinary criminal courts and courts-martial.

The Court found that Section 549(1) Cr.P.C. should be interpreted in light of Section 125 of the Army Act, as both provisions share the objective of preventing jurisdictional conflicts between the two types of courts.

The Court determined that the word "jurisdiction" in the related Section 125 of the Army Act signifies the initial jurisdiction to take cognizance of a case, not the jurisdiction to decide it on its merits.

application.fact_text: The Court interpreted the clause "for which he is liable to be tried either by the court to which this Code applies or by a court-martial" as qualifying the preceding part of the section, "when any person is charged with an offence."
Based on this, the Court reasoned that the phrase "liable to be tried" means that the offence must be one of which both an ordinary criminal court and a court-martial can take cognizance.

The Court explicitly stated its opinion that the phrase is intended to refer to the initial jurisdiction of the two courts to take cognizance of the case, not their jurisdiction to decide it on the merits.
The Court rejected the alternative argument that the phrase required a court to have jurisdiction not only at the initial stage but also through to the final stage of conviction or acquittal.
By applying the same construction used for Section 125 of the Army Act, the Court concluded that both provisions refer to the initial stage at which proceedings are instituted.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the phrase 'liable to be tried' in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code refers to the initial jurisdiction of a court to take cognizance of a case, not its jurisdiction to try the case and decide it on its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the procedure specified in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code and the rules made thereunder is mandatory in cases where both an ordinary criminal court and a court-martial have concurrent jurisdiction.

facts: An army officer was charged by a Special Judge with offences under the Indian Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act.
It was admitted that both the ordinary criminal court and the court-martial had concurrent jurisdiction over the offences with which the officer was charged.
The Special Judge framed charges against the officer without following the procedure laid out in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) and its associated rules.
law: Section 549(1) Cr.P.C. provides a procedure for cases where a person is subject to military law and is charged with an offence for which they can be tried by either a criminal court or a court-martial.
Section 125 of the Army Act gives the commanding officer discretion to decide before which court (criminal court or court-martial) proceedings should be instituted when both have jurisdiction.
The purpose of both Section 549(1) Cr.P.C. and Section 125 of the Army Act is to avoid a conflict of jurisdiction between the two court systems.
application: The Court interpreted the key phrase in Section 549(1), "liable to be tried either by a court to which this Code applies or by a court-martial," to refer to the *initial jurisdiction* of the two courts to take cognizance of a case, not their jurisdiction to decide the case on its merits.
The Court reasoned that this interpretation is consistent with Section 125 of the Army Act, which also deals with the initial stage of instituting proceedings.
The Court rejected the argument that both courts must retain jurisdiction until the final stage of conviction or acquittal for the procedure to apply.

Since it was an admitted fact that both the criminal court and the court-martial had concurrent initial jurisdiction to take cognizance of the case, the conditions for applying Section 549(1) were met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the procedure specified in Section 549(1) Cr.P.C. and the rules made thereunder was mandatory in this case. Because both the ordinary criminal court and the court-martial had concurrent jurisdiction to initially take cognizance of the offences, the procedure designed to avoid jurisdictional conflict was attracted and had to be followed by the Special Judge.

issue.issue_text: Whether the issue of limitation under Section 122 of the Army Act is to be decided by the ordinary criminal court or by the court-martial itself.

facts: An army officer was charged in a special criminal court for offences committed in 1962, but the charges were framed in 1967, more than three years later.

The prosecution argued that because the three-year limitation period for a court-martial under Section 122(1) of the Army Act had expired, the court-martial no longer had jurisdiction to try the case.
Based on this, the prosecution contended that the ordinary criminal court could proceed with the trial without following the procedures for cases of concurrent jurisdiction.

law.description: States that no trial by court-martial shall be commenced after the expiry of three years from the date of the offence.
Provides that in computing the three-year period, any time the accused spent evading arrest shall be excluded.
Grants the commanding officer the discretion to decide whether proceedings should be instituted in a criminal court or a court-martial when both have jurisdiction.
Allows the Central Government to sanction a trial in an ordinary criminal court if a court-martial has already acquitted or convicted the person, or found it cannot try them.

application: The Court determined that the question of jurisdiction in this context refers to the initial authority to take cognizance of a case, not the final power to convict or acquit.

The Court reasoned that the issue of limitation under Section 122 is not a simple matter of dates. It involves a factual inquiry, particularly under sub-section (3), to determine if the accused was evading arrest, which would pause the limitation period.

The Court held that this factual determination is an integral part of the trial itself. Since the court-martial has the initial jurisdiction to begin an inquiry, it is the only competent body to decide whether it retains jurisdiction to proceed with the full trial.

The Court referred to this as a "conjoint reading" of sub-sections (1) and (3) of Section 122, which makes it evident that the court-martial, not the ordinary criminal court, must decide the limitation issue.

Furthermore, the Court noted that if the court-martial finds it cannot try the case due to the time limit, the accused does not automatically go free. Section 127 provides a procedure for the Central Government to then sanction a trial in an ordinary criminal court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the court-martial itself, and not the ordinary criminal court, has the jurisdiction to decide the issue of limitation under Section 122 of the Army Act. This determination is considered a part of the trial before the court-martial.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code is inapplicable to a case where a court-martial's jurisdiction is potentially barred by the limitation period under Section 122 of the Army Act.

facts: An army officer was charged in a civilian criminal court in 1967 for offences committed in 1962.
The appellant argued that since more than three years had passed, the court-martial's jurisdiction was barred by the limitation period in Section 122(1) of the Army Act.
Based on this, the appellant contended that Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), which governs cases of concurrent jurisdiction, was not applicable.
law: Section 549(1) Cr.P.C. provides a procedure to decide whether a person subject to military law should be tried by a civilian court or a court-martial when both have jurisdiction.
Section 122(1) of the Army Act states that a trial by court-martial cannot commence after three years from the date of the offence.
Section 122(3) of the Army Act allows for the exclusion of time spent evading arrest when calculating the three-year limitation period.
Section 125 of the Army Act gives a commanding officer discretion to decide the venue of the trial when both a criminal court and a court-martial have jurisdiction.
application: The Court interpreted the phrase "liable to be tried" in Section 549(1) Cr.P.C. and the word "jurisdiction" in Section 125 of the Army Act as referring to the *initial jurisdiction to take cognizance* of a case, not the jurisdiction to decide it on the merits.
It was admitted that both the civilian court and the court-martial had initial concurrent jurisdiction over the offences themselves, which is the trigger for applying Section 549(1).
The Court reasoned that the question of whether the trial was barred by the three-year limitation period was a matter for the court-martial itself to decide, not the civilian court.
This is because the court-martial is the competent authority to determine factual issues that affect the limitation period, such as whether the accused was evading arrest (as per Section 122(3)).

Therefore, the potential limitation bar is a defense to be raised during the trial at the court-martial, not a reason to bypass the initial procedure under Section 549(1) for determining which court should hear the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code was applicable. The potential time bar under the Army Act does not eliminate the court-martial's initial jurisdiction; rather, the issue of limitation is a matter for the court-martial itself to decide as part of the trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'liable to be tried' in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code refers to the initial jurisdiction of a court to take cognizance of a case, or its jurisdiction to decide the case on its merits.
appellant_arguments: The phrase 'liable to be tried' connotes that the court-martial must have jurisdiction to decide the case on its merits, not just concurrent initial jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence.
respondent_arguments: The phrase 'liable to be tried' refers to the initial jurisdiction of both the ordinary criminal court and the court-martial to take cognizance of the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the procedure specified in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code and the rules made thereunder is mandatory in cases where both an ordinary criminal court and a court-martial have concurrent jurisdiction.
appellant_arguments: The procedure under Section 549(1) was not applicable in this specific case because the respondent was not 'liable to be tried' by a court-martial due to other legal bars (like limitation).
respondent_arguments: The procedure specified in Section 549(1) and the rules made thereunder (Rule 3) are mandatory, and failure by the Special Judge to follow this procedure before framing charges means the charges cannot survive.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the issue of limitation under Section 122 of the Army Act is to be decided by the ordinary criminal court or by the court-martial itself.
appellant_arguments: The ordinary criminal court should consider the issue of limitation under the Army Act to determine if an accused is truly 'liable to be tried' by a court-martial before applying the procedure of Section 549(1).
respondent_arguments: The question of limitation is a matter of merit to be decided by the court-martial itself, and should not be pre-judged by the ordinary criminal court to bypass the mandatory procedure for choosing the forum under Section 549(1).

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code is inapplicable to a case where a court-martial's jurisdiction is potentially barred by the limitation period under Section 122 of the Army Act.
appellant_arguments: In the particular circumstances of this case, where a trial by court-martial is potentially barred by limitation, the respondent is not 'liable to be tried' by it, and therefore Section 549(1) is not applicable.
respondent_arguments: The applicability of Section 549(1) is based on the concurrent initial jurisdiction over the offence, and a potential limitation bar does not make the section inapplicable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a person subject to military law is brought before a criminal court for an offense over which both the criminal court and a court-martial have concurrent jurisdiction, the procedure specified in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code and the rules made thereunder is mandatory. The phrase 'liable to be tried' refers to the initial jurisdiction of the courts to take cognizance of the case, not their jurisdiction to decide it on the merits. Charges framed by the criminal court without following this mandatory procedure cannot stand and must be quashed.
obiter: The court-martial alone has jurisdiction to decide the issue of limitation under Section 122(1) of the Army Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The procedure specified in Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code and the rules made thereunder is mandatory. Where a person is subject to both military and civilian law for an offence, the ordinary criminal court must follow this procedure to determine which forum will conduct the trial. Because the Special Judge framed charges without following this mandatory procedure, the charges cannot stand and must be quashed.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation: The court interpreted Section 549(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code in conjunction with Section 125 of the Army Act, reasoning that since both provisions aim to avoid conflicts of jurisdiction between civilian courts and courts-martial, they should be given a similar construction.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's interpretation of the phrase 'liable to be tried', stating: 'We are unable to accept this construction of the phrase... the phrase is intended to refer to the initial jurisdiction of the two courts to take cognizance of the case and not to their jurisdiction to decide it on merits.'

The appellant's argument that a potential limitation bar under the Army Act makes Section 549(1) inapplicable was rejected because the court held that the issue of limitation is a matter for the court-martial itself to decide, not a precondition for the criminal court to consider. The court noted: 'Section 125 supports our view that the court-martial alone has jurisdiction to decide the issue of limitation under s. 122(1).'
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that the procedure under Section 549(1) Cr.P.C. and its associated rules is mandatory, and the Special Judge's failure to follow it was fatal to the charges. The court stated: 'It is ar. admitted fact in this case that the procedure specified in rule 3 was not followed by the Special Judge, Gauhati before framing charges against the respondent. Section 549 (1) Cr.P.C. ;111d rule 3 are mand;1tory. Accordingly the charges, framed by the Special Judge against the respondent cannot survive.'

The court accepted the respondent's position that 'liable to be tried' refers to the existence of concurrent initial jurisdiction, not the ultimate ability to secure a conviction. The court reasoned: 'the phrase "is liable to be tried either by a court to which this Code applie' or a court-martial" imports that the offence for which the accused is to be tried should be an offence of which cognizance can be taken by an ordinary criminal court as well as a court'martial.'
policy_considerations: The primary policy consideration is the need to prevent procedural conflicts when two judicial systems have concurrent jurisdiction over an offence. The court stated: 'Section 549 (1) Cr. P .C. is designed to avoid the conflict of jurisdiction in respect of the last category of offences.' and 'Both the provisions have in mind th·~ object of avoiding a collision between the ordinary criminal court and the court- martial.'
